question.text:
You are a portfolio manager provided with the expected return and standard deviation of four assets. Asset A: Expected Mean Return: 5%, Standard Deviation: 0; Asset B: Expected Mean Return: 10%, Standard Deviation: 10%; Asset C: Expected Mean Return: 12%, Standard Deviation: 15%; Asset D: Expected Mean Return: 7%, Standard Deviation: 17%.
If you could invest in only one of the three assets (A, B, or C), which one would you pick?

answer.text: Any of them depending upon the risk profile of the investor and investment objectives

explanation.text: The Logic: Without knowing the investor's risk profile, objectives and risk-return profile, no single asset among A, B and C is universally best. Asset A's zero standard deviation suits a risk-averse investor; Asset C's 12% expected return suits a more aggressive investor; Asset B (10% return, 10% SD) sits in between. The workbook makes the IPS, risk profiling, objectives and risk-return profile the drivers of strategy selection, and higher standard deviation is treated as higher risk — so the suitable choice is conditional on the client. The Trap: Picking A purely because zero SD feels "safe", C because 12% is the highest headline number, or B as the balanced middle — each is right only for a specific profile. Choosing any single asset without the client's risk tolerance is the classic product-push trap. Note: Source — NISM-Series-XXI-A workbook (September 2025), pages 123, 125 and 131 (IPS, risk profiling, objectives and risk-return profile driving investment strategy) and page 147 (higher standard deviation means higher risk).
